findings.message: Two different things are called 'the note'. In the locker, Ivy takes 'the note' off the tag (story.r6.json, passage locker, paragraph 4). The locked hint and choice label at threshold say 'the last log note'. A young reader could mix them up. Suggest 'the tag' in the locker.

The locked choice 'open-careful' has a hint ('Find a long pole and read the last log note first.'), but by that point no route lets the reader go back. They must replay from the start. That is fair for a replayable story, and nothing forces backtracking, but the hint could say it is for the next read.
The passage title 'The Door Hisses' differs from the ending title 'Too Fast' (passage title, and ending.title in ending-rush). Cosmetic; make them match.

Skills practised: the story practises decoding in context (vowel-team, silent-e and th words recur on every ending route), recognising the same word-set words in narration and in choice labels, and following a three-step sequence (Nib's chalk steps) where order matters. Readers also infer from clues (a log note dated four days ago on a ship lost eleven years ago, one live cable running to the cargo door), learn words such as corridor, valve and beacon from context and the glossary, and use evidence to weigh a risk before choosing an ending. Limits: this review rests on spelling-based detection, which cannot confirm how a word sounds, and on a read of the text, not a test with a reader.

Comprehension gap: 'the blue tube' is used as a tool (Nib's step One in 'nib'; 'Cool the lock with the blue tube first' in 'climax-careful'; Bo cools the lock in 'hold-open' and 'climax-team'), but it is never introduced or found. The reader also has a different 'tube' (the dock tube) in mind from 'start' and 'tube'. This looks like word-set weaving that outran the plot. Suggest the narrative designer introduce the blue tube once (for example in 'locker' or 'engine') or rename it so it is not confused with the dock tube.

Continuity slip that can confuse a reader: the choice 'Carry the moths home in the Kestrel's dome' (climax-team) and the line 'packed the moths into the Kestrel's dome' (ending-carry) assume the Kestrel has a dome. Only the Lark's glass dome ('dome') is established. Suggest the narrative designer say 'a glass case' or add a dome to the Kestrel earlier.

The rush route reads oddly after 'climax-careful': choosing 'Lift the door first, to see inside' leads to 'ending-rush', whose first line says 'The team rushed the lock'. The reader has not tried to cut a lock on this route, and the cause-and-effect link is weaker than on the 'open-rush' route. Suggest a one-line change so the ending names the cause for either entry. Also, the lockedHint ('Find a long pole and read the last log note first.') is clear, but players who took 'hull-check' never get the 'late-log' clue and can only unlock 'open-careful' by going back, which is not a path in this graph. Those players see the choice locked with no way to meet its needs. Suggest the narrative designer check that this is intended.

The glossary words salvage and derelict are good, but a short in-text use would help.

shelfSummary.blurb: A space salvage mystery with five endings. Readers practise vowel team, silent-e and th words, with r-controlled, blend, -ed and ck words too, while using clues, sequencing and vocabulary from context to decide how to open a sealed hold.

findings.message: Skills practised: the story practises decoding in context (vowel-team, silent-e and th-digraph words recur on the shortest route to every one of the five endings, and I traced several full routes by hand, including ones through the four passages rewritten in this revision — 'hull-marks', 'porthole', 'engine-trace' and 'nib-ask' — and confirmed the same word-set words carry through them), recognising set words in both narration and choice labels, and following a three-step sequence (Nib's chalk steps: cool the lock, turn the valve, lift the door) where order matters. Readers also infer from clues (a log note dated four days ago on a ship lost eleven years ago; one live cable running to the cargo door), learn words such as corridor, valve and beacon from context and the glossary, and weigh evidence before choosing an ending. Limits: this review and the automated report both detect patterns by spelling, not sound, so a match (for example 'th' in 'that' and 'thin') does not prove a given reader pronounces it as intended, and nothing here is a substitute for a human reading check with an actual learner.

The four newly rewritten connector passages carry real word-set practice rather than diluting it. 'hull-marks' adds 'thin', 'that', 'team' and 'tube'; 'porthole' adds 'dome', 'moth' and 'keep' (all three target patterns in one short passage); 'engine-trace' adds 'thin', 'pole' and 'hope'; 'nib-ask' adds 'keep', 'them' and 'that'. Each word still carries its declared pattern and reads naturally in the new sentences (e.g. porthole: "Let's keep moving"). The second choice added to each of these four passages (to satisfy the graph validator's two-choice rule) does not introduce any new word-set word that fails its pattern, and does not remove set words from the passages that already existed in r6. Per-word totals actually improved slightly from the prior reviewed revision: 'keep' rose from roughly 2 to 4 occurrences because of 'porthole' and 'nib-ask'.

Comprehension gap, carried over from the r6 review and still present in r8: 'the blue tube' is used as a tool to cool the cargo-door lock (Nib's step one in 'nib'; the choice label 'Cool the lock with the blue tube first' in 'climax-careful'; Bo cooling the lock with it in 'hold-open' and 'climax-team'), but this tool is never introduced, found or named as an item anywhere in the story — it only appears in dialogue and steps. This also collides with the unrelated 'dock tube' the crew already crawled through in 'start' and 'tube', so an attentive reader may expect it to be the same object. Suggest the narrative designer introduce a tool called the blue tube (for example in 'locker', alongside the hook-pole) or rename one of the two tubes.

Continuity slip, carried over from r6 and still present in r8: the choice 'Carry the moths home in the Kestrel's dome' (climax-team) and the line 'packed the moths into the Kestrel's dome' (ending-carry) both assume the salvage tug Kestrel has a glass dome, but only the Lark's dome is established anywhere in the story ('dome', 'inside'). Suggest 'a glass case' or similar on the Kestrel, or an earlier line establishing the Kestrel also has one.

Design gap, carried over from r6 and still present in r8: the 'late-log' clue is only granted in 'log-read' (reached only via scan -> read-log). A reader who instead takes scan -> check-hull, or skips 'scan' entirely via start -> tube, can never collect 'late-log' and so can never satisfy the locked choice 'open-careful' at 'threshold', even though its lockedHint ('Find a long pole and read the last log note first.') reads as still achievable. This is a plot/branching design question for the narrative designer, not a word-set defect, and it does not block this review, since the other four endings remain fully reachable with full word-set coverage.

Word coverage is met with a wide margin (vowel-team 31/10, silent-e 48/8, th 57/8) but still thin for a few individual words: 'rain' (2: 'scan', 'climax-team'), 'boat' (2: 'nib', 'ending-tow') and 'cave' (2: 'threshold', 'ending-garden'). These are unchanged from the r6 review; the r7/r8 connector fixes added occurrences of 'keep', 'dome', 'thin', 'that', 'them' and 'tube' but did not touch 'rain', 'boat' or 'cave'. This does not block the pass; I confirm (by my own hand-trace of several routes, not only the automated report) that every set still appears well before the minimum on every route I checked, including the four rewritten connectors.

The declared th-words set mixes two different 'th' sounds under one spelling: voiceless in 'thin', 'thud', 'path' and 'moth', voiced in 'that' and 'them'. Spelling-pattern detection (both the automated report and my own reading) cannot tell these apart, so a pass on this word set confirms the spelling pattern only, not that a given reader will hear or produce the same sound for every instance. A program that teaches these as two separate sounds may want to treat 'that'/'them' and the four voiceless words as separate practice sets when mapping this story to its own terms.

shelfSummary.blurb: A salvage crew finds a drifting ship, a sealed cargo door and a log note written years after the ship went silent. Reading the clues and going slowly pays off; rushing in brings a setback instead.

findings.message: The two new choices added to fix the engine-trace single-choice error (story.r8.json lines 373-385, choices "trace-on" and "call-out") both target "nib" with no requires/effects difference between them. They are not a genuine branch point: whichever label the reader picks, the next passage, state, items and clues are identical. This clears the automated graph check but not the underlying problem it was flagging (give the reader a real decision), and it does not match the stated intent of revision 8 ("connector passages fixed, zero single-choice" implying real branching, not a cosmetic duplicate).

Same defect in the nib-ask connector (story.r8.json lines 423-435, choices "nib-ask-on" and "promise-nib"): both target "threshold" with no state difference. The "promise-nib" label ("Promise Nib you will be careful, then go to the door") implies a consequence, but no flag, item, clue or later passage ever reflects the promise - it is cosmetic filler added only to satisfy the single-choice validator, not a real decision.

By contrast, the other two passages revision 8 was meant to fix are genuine fixes: hull-marks (lines 164-186) now forks to "tube" vs "locker" (a real shortcut that changes which passages are read and whether hook-pole is picked up on that path), and porthole (lines ~243-262) forks to "inside" vs "dome" (skips the quiet-corridor passage). These two are fine and should be the model for fixing engine-trace and nib-ask the same way, e.g. by giving one option a distinct destination or a distinct item/clue/flag effect.

Skills practised: the story practises decoding in context (vowel-team, silent-e and th-digraph words recur on the shortest route to every one of the five endings, and I re-traced routes through the two passages this revision touched, 'engine-trace' and 'nib-ask', confirming word-set words still carry through them), recognising set words in both narration and choice labels, and following a three-step sequence (Nib's chalk steps: cool the lock with the blue tube, turn the valve, lift the door) where order matters. Readers also infer from clues (a log note four days old on a ship lost eleven years ago; a soft repeating thud behind a blinking box), learn words such as corridor, valve and beacon from context and the glossary, and weigh evidence before choosing one of five endings. Limits: this review and the automated report both detect patterns by spelling, not sound, so a match (for example 'th' in 'thud' versus 'that') does not prove a given reader pronounces it as intended, and nothing here substitutes for a human reading check with an actual learner.

Verified independently against reports/literacy.r8.json and reports/literacy.r9.json (not just the author's revision notes): vowel-team-words rose 31->33 (perWord 'keep' 4->6), silent-e-words rose 48->50 (perWord 'note' 10->12), th-words rose 57->59 (perWord 'thud' 4->5, 'path' 7->8). No word fell below the brief's per-set minimums (10/8/8) and none dropped out; the automated report confirms meetsMinimum:true and missingWords:[] for all three sets on r9, and perEndingRoute shows every set still present on all five routes (ending-garden/-carry/-tow/-closed/-rush). The new words read naturally and carry their declared pattern in context: 'thud' in 'Then it gave a soft thud, twice, like a secret code.' (engine-trace), 'path' in the relabelled choice 'Follow the cable's path to the light' (engine-trace, trace-on), 'keep' in 'Call out, and keep listening for an answer' (engine-trace, call-out), and 'note'/'keep' in the relabelled choice 'Promise to keep the chalk note safe, then take it' (nib-ask, promise-nib). conceptMismatches is empty for all three sets, confirming the automated spelling check as well.

The revision notes attribute the vowel-team increase to the new 'keep' in engine-trace's call-out label only, but there is a second new 'keep' in nib-ask's relabelled promise-nib choice ('Promise to keep the chalk note safe, then take it'), which is where the +2 total actually comes from. This is a documentation gap in the notes, not a defect in the story: both instances are natural and correctly carry the vowel-team pattern, and the reported totals (33/50/59) are correct either way.

The two new state-bearing effects read as genuine, player-visible differences rather than cosmetic filler, resolving the QA findings on r8. In engine-trace, only 'call-out' grants the clue 'blink-code' ('The blinking code'); 'trace-on' does not. In nib-ask, only 'promise-nib' grants the item 'chalk-note' ("Nib's chalk note"); 'nib-ask-on' does not. Both additions are flavour/collectible only (neither is referenced by any 'requires'), so they cannot create a new soft-lock, matching the author's stated intent. This is a QA/engine-trace concern more than a literacy one, but it is relevant to comprehension: the new closing line in each passage ('a soft thud, twice, like a secret code' and 'Nib snapped off a small chalk note and held it out, like a gift') is what motivates the new choice, so the branch now makes narrative sense as well as mechanical sense.

Carried over from the r8 literacy review (work/literacy-review.r8.json) and still present, unchanged, in r9 because neither passage was touched by this revision: (1) 'the blue tube' is used as the tool that cools the cargo-door lock (in 'nib', the choice label in 'climax-careful', and the narration in 'hold-open'/'climax-team'), but it is never introduced or found as an item anywhere in the story, and it risks being read as the same object as the unrelated 'dock tube' from 'start'/'tube'. (2) 'Carry the moths home in the Kestrel's dome' (climax-team) and 'packed the moths into the Kestrel's dome' (ending-carry) assume the tug Kestrel has a glass dome, but only the Lark's dome is established elsewhere in the story. Neither issue is a word-set defect and neither blocks this pass, but both remain open comprehension/continuity gaps for the narrative designer.

Also carried over and unchanged: the 'late-log' clue is only granted in 'log-read', reachable only via start->scan->log-read. A reader who takes scan->check-hull, or skips 'scan' via start->tube, can never collect 'late-log' and so can never take the locked choice 'open-careful' at 'threshold', even though its lockedHint ('Find a long pole and read the last log note first.') reads as still achievable from any route. This is a branching design question for the narrative designer, not a word-set defect; the other four endings remain fully reachable with full word-set coverage regardless.

Coverage is comfortably above minimum on all three sets (33/10, 50/8, 59/8) but a few individual words are still thin and unchanged by this revision: 'rain' (2 occurrences: 'scan', 'climax-team'), 'boat' (2: 'nib', 'ending-tow') and 'cave' (2: 'threshold', 'ending-garden'). This does not block the pass; every set still appears well before its minimum on every route, including the two rewritten connectors.

The declared th-words set mixes two different 'th' sounds under one spelling pattern: voiceless in 'thin', 'thud', 'path' and 'moth', voiced in 'that' and 'them'. Both the automated report and my own reading detect spelling only, so a pass on this word set confirms the spelling pattern, not that a given reader will hear or produce the same sound for every instance (for example the new 'thud' and the pre-existing 'that' are spelled alike but sound different). A structured-literacy program that teaches these as two separate sounds may want to split 'that'/'them' from the four voiceless words when mapping this story to its own terms.
